word: Bless the LORD, O My Soul
pronunciation: BLES thuh LORD oh my SOHL
pos: n. phr. (David's self-address, the frame of Psalms 103 and 104)
etymology: Hebrew bār'kī naphshī 'eth-YHWH — bārak, to kneel and so to bless; nephesh, the soul or whole living self, here addressed in the second person by the man who owns it.
biblical_def: The clause opens and closes Psalm 103 and opens and closes Psalm 104, so that two of the Psalter's greatest songs are bracketed by it. The striking thing is its grammar: David is not addressing God and not addressing a congregation but himself. Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. This is a man commanding his own inner life to do what it ought and is not doing, and Scripture does it often — Why art thou cast down, O my soul? — and answers it with hope thou in God. The assumption is that the affections are not sovereign over the believer; he may address them, reason with them and order them, and praise is therefore a duty that can be taken up before it is felt. The psalm then supplies the fuel, since a soul commanded to bless must be given grounds: forgiveth all thine iniquities, healeth all thy diseases, redeemeth thy life from destruction, crowneth thee with lovingkindness. And the second line guards against half-measures — all that is within me. To bless God is not to confer a benefit on Him, for nothing can be added to Him; the Hebrew root is to kneel, and the creature's blessing of God is the acknowledgment of what He already is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Bless, to praise; to glorify for benefits received. Soul, the spiritual, rational and immortal substance in man. Psalm 103:1, the believer commanding his own soul to praise.
webster_full: Bless, to praise; to glorify for benefits received; to extol for excellencies.
Bless, to wish happiness to another; to make happy; to bestow prosperity on.
Soul, the spiritual, rational and immortal substance in man which distinguishes him from brutes.
Hebrew bārak, to kneel, and hence to bless or salute.
Hebrew nephesh, the soul, the life, the whole living self. Psalm 103:1.
scriptures: A Psalm of David. Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name.
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases;
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
corruption_summary: Praise is treated as valid only when spontaneous, so a commanded blessing is called insincere; or blessing God is imagined to add something to Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is that worship must be felt to be real, and that to summon praise from an unwilling heart is hypocrisy. The Psalter assumes the opposite. David speaks to his soul in the imperative because the soul is sluggish and needs addressing, and the same psalmist elsewhere interrogates his own despondency and prescribes hope to it. The believer is not the passive spectator of his own affections; he is responsible for them, and may preach to himself before breakfast. A praise begun as duty and warmed by rehearsing God's benefits is not insincere — it is the ordinary way the heart is brought round.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what blessing God means. To bless a man is to wish and work good toward him, and nothing in that sense can be rendered to God, who is blessed for ever and lacks nothing. The Hebrew root is to kneel, and the creature's blessing is confession: naming aloud what God is and what He has done. The second half of the psalm's frame makes it plain by widening the summons — bless the LORD, ye His angels, ye His hosts, all His works in all places of His dominion — before returning, in the last line, to the single soul where it began.
roots_summary: Hebrew bārak, to kneel and so to bless, with nephesh, the whole living self — a man ordering his own soul to praise, and then supplying it reasons.
roots_lines: Hebrew bārak, to kneel; hence to bless, salute, or praise.
Hebrew nephesh, soul, life, the whole person as a living being.
The clause frames both Psalm 103 and Psalm 104, opening and closing each.
All that is within me forbids a divided or partial praise.
Compare the same self-address in Psalm 42:11 — hope thou in God.
usage: Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name
forget not all his benefits
who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases

word: If I Forget Thee, O Jerusalem
pronunciation: if y for-GET thee oh juh-ROO-suh-lum
pos: n. phr. (the exiles' oath by the rivers of Babylon, Psalm 137:5)
etymology: Hebrew 'im-'eshkāchēk y'rūshālaim — the conditional 'im introduces a self-imprecatory oath, the second half of which calls down the penalty: tishkach y'mīnī, let my right hand forget.
biblical_def: Psalm 137 is the Psalter's one song written beside a foreign river. The exiles have hung their harps on the willows, because their captors required of them a song and mirth — sing us one of the songs of Zion — and the psalmist asks how they should sing the LORD's song in a strange land. Then comes the oath: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning. The oath is doubled in the verse that follows — If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy. The form is self-imprecation: the singer calls down on himself the loss of the hand that plays and the tongue that sings, the two instruments of the very art his captors are demanding. The oath is not nostalgia for a hometown. Jerusalem was the place of the temple, the ark, the sacrifices and the promise to David, so to forget Jerusalem was to forget the covenant and the God who made it. The refusal to perform the songs of Zion as entertainment, and the vow to prefer that city above his chief joy, are therefore one act of faith: the exile will not let the worship of God be reduced to a captor's amusement, and will not let distance make him forget.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Forget, to lose the remembrance of. Cunning, knowledge; skill; dexterity in performance. Psalm 137:5, the exile's self-imprecatory oath.
webster_full: Forget, to lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory.
Cunning, knowledge; art; skill; dexterity in the performance of a thing.
Captivity, the state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy.
Hebrew shākach, to forget, cease to care for, ignore.
Hebrew dābaq, to cleave or cling — the tongue to the roof of the mouth. Psalm 137:6.
scriptures: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy.
corruption_summary: The oath is read as mere patriotism or ethnic sentiment, and the psalm as a whole is dismissed for its closing imprecation rather than handled as inspired Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Reduced to homesickness, the verse becomes a model for loving one's country and nothing more. The singer's subject is not a landscape but a covenant: Jerusalem held the house where God had put His name, and the songs the captors wanted were the songs of Zion, worship wrenched out of its setting and sold as entertainment. The modern parallel is exact enough to be uncomfortable — sacred song performed for an audience that wants the sound and not the God — and the psalmist's answer is to hang up the harp rather than oblige.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover concerns the psalm's ending, which is now the reason it is most often skipped: the blessing pronounced on him that dasheth the little ones against the stones. It is an imprecation, it is inspired, and it is a prayer that God will do what He had already declared through Isaiah that He would do to Babylon. It is not a licence for private vengeance — the psalmist asks God to act and does not act himself — and it belongs to the same Scripture that forbids the believer to avenge himself. An editor who keeps verses one to six and drops the rest has decided he is a better judge than the Spirit who gave the whole.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'im, introducing a self-imprecatory oath — the hand and tongue forfeited if Jerusalem, and so the covenant, is forgotten.
roots_lines: Hebrew shākach, to forget or cease to care for.
The particle 'im opens a conditional self-curse, with the penalty named after.
Hebrew dābaq, to cleave; the tongue to the palate, Psalm 137:6.
The forfeits are the harpist's hand and the singer's tongue — the captors' demand.
Jerusalem stands for the temple, the covenant and the promise to David.
usage: if I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning
how shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?
if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy

word: A Lamp Unto My Feet, and a Light Unto My Path
pronunciation: uh LAMP UN-too my FEET and uh LYT UN-too my PATH
pos: n. phr. (the NUN stanza of the great psalm of the word, Psalm 119:105)
etymology: Hebrew nēr-l'raglī d'bārekhā w''ōr lin'thībāthī — nēr, the small clay hand-lamp, not a torch or beacon; n'thībāh, a beaten footpath rather than a highway.
biblical_def: The verse opens the NUN stanza of Psalm 119, the long acrostic meditation on the word of God, and its figures are chosen with care. A nēr is the small oil lamp a traveller carried in his hand or tied at his ankle; it did not light the countryside, it lit the next step. The parallel noun is a footpath, not a road. So the promise of the verse is deliberately modest and exactly sufficient: Scripture is given not to satisfy curiosity about the whole journey but to show a man where to put his foot now. That is why the psalm surrounds the verse with vows rather than speculations — I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments; I am afflicted very much: quicken me, O LORD, according unto thy word. The lamp is for walking by. Two doctrines follow. The sufficiency of Scripture is real but is a sufficiency for the way God has appointed, which is obedience, and not for every question a man might raise. And the illumination is personal: the lamp is at my feet and the path is my path, so the word must be taken up and carried, not admired at a distance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Lamp, a vessel with a wick for burning oil. Path, a way beaten by the feet of man or beast. Psalm 119:105, the word that lights the next step.
webster_full: Lamp, a vessel with a wick, used for the combustion of oil or other inflammable substance.
Lamp, figuratively, a light; a source of illumination or instruction.
Path, a way beaten by the feet of man or beast; a narrow way to be passed on foot.
Hebrew nēr, a small hand-lamp of clay, carried by a traveller.
Hebrew n'thībāh, a footpath or trodden way. Psalm 119:105.
scriptures: NUN. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: The verse is made a promise of detailed private guidance about decisions Scripture never addresses, or the lamp is supplemented by impressions and inner voices treated as equally authoritative.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest misuse turns the lamp into an oracle for personal decisions — which job, which house, which person — and then, when Scripture is silent on the question, fills the silence with impressions, open doors and fleeces, which are credited with the same authority as the text. The verse promises light for the path, and the path in Psalm 119 is the way of God's commandments; the stanza that contains it is full of vows to keep His judgments, not of requests for information. A believer facing a lawful choice between lawful options has not been abandoned by the lamp; he has been given wisdom, counsel and liberty, and the lamp shows him how to walk whichever way he goes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the modesty of the figure, which is also its comfort. Men want a floodlight over the whole road and are given a hand-lamp over the next yard, and they call this insufficient. Peter calls the prophetic word a light that shineth in a dark place, and bids us take heed to it until the day dawn; the dimness is the condition of the present age, not a defect in the lamp. The light that is given is enough to walk by, and walking is what it was given for.
roots_summary: Hebrew nēr, the traveller's small hand-lamp, over n'thībāh, a footpath — light for the next step, not for the whole journey.
roots_lines: Hebrew nēr, a small clay lamp carried in the hand or at the ankle.
Hebrew 'ōr, light; dābār, word — the word itself is the lamp.
Hebrew n'thībāh, a beaten footpath, not a highway.
The stanza answers with a vow, not a question: Psalm 119:106.
Peter's parallel: a light that shineth in a dark place, 2 Peter 1:19.
usage: thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path
I have sworn, and I will perform it, that I will keep thy righteous judgments
the entrance of thy words giveth light

word: From the Rising of the Sun Unto the Going Down of the Same
pronunciation: from thuh RY-zing uv thuh SUN UN-too thuh GOH-ing DOWN uv thuh SAYM
pos: n. phr. (the compass of the LORD's praise, Psalm 113:3)
etymology: Hebrew mimmizrach-shemesh 'ad-m'bō'ō — from the sun's rising to its going in; the idiom is spatial, east to west, and by extension temporal, dawn to dusk.
biblical_def: The clause belongs to the first of the Hallel psalms: From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD's name is to be praised. The Hebrew idiom is primarily geographical — from the east where the sun comes up to the west where it goes in, which is to say everywhere the sun touches — and because the same words describe a day, the phrase carries both reaches at once: all places and all hours. The psalm sets it between two statements that explain it. Before it: blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and for evermore, which adds all ages to all places. After it: the LORD is high above all nations, and His glory above the heavens. Malachi takes the identical idiom and makes it a prophecy rather than a summons — from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same, My name shall be great among the Gentiles, and in every place incense shall be offered unto My name and a pure offering. Spoken to a priesthood that was offering polluted bread on the LORD's own altar, the sentence is a warning as much as a promise: the praise will be universal with Israel or without her.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Rising, the act of getting up; appearance above the horizon. Going down, descent; setting. Psalm 113:3, praise as wide as the sun's circuit.
webster_full: Rising, the act of mounting or ascending; the appearance of the sun above the horizon.
Going down, the act of descending; the setting of the sun.
Praise, to commend; to applaud; to extol in words or song, as the perfections of God.
Hebrew mizrach, the east or sun-rising; mābō', the entrance or going in.
The same idiom in Malachi 1:11, of the Gentiles' pure offering.
scriptures: Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and for evermore.
From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD'S name is to be praised.
The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens.
Mal 1:11

For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering: for my name shall be great among the heathen, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: The clause is reduced to a figure for daily devotional habit, losing the geographic claim; or Malachi's use of it is read as endorsing the worship offered by the nations in their own religions.
corruption_paragraphs: Taken only temporally, the verse becomes a call to pray morning and evening, which is good counsel and much less than the text says. The idiom is first of all a map: east to west, the whole inhabited earth under the sun's circuit. The psalm proves the reading in its next line by lifting the LORD above all nations, and the Hallel as a whole moves outward from Israel's deliverance to the dominion of her God. A reading that keeps the hours and drops the nations has halved the verse.

The more serious misuse belongs to Malachi 1:11, which has been pressed into service for the view that sincere worship in any religion rises acceptably to the one God, since incense is said to be offered to His name in every place. The chapter is against it from end to end. Malachi is rebuking priests who bring the blind and the lame to the altar, and his argument is comparative shame: the LORD will have a pure offering from the Gentiles while Israel's own priests despise His table. The offering foretold is pure, it is to His name, and the New Testament identifies its substance — the sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips giving thanks, offered through Jesus Christ. The principle to recover is that the universality of the praise is the reach of the gospel, not the validity of the religions.
roots_summary: Hebrew mimmizrach-shemesh 'ad-m'bō'ō — east to west, and so dawn to dusk: all places and all hours under one Name.
roots_lines: Hebrew mizrach, the east, the place of the sun's rising.
Hebrew mābō', the entrance or going in; of the sun, its setting.
The idiom is spatial first, temporal by extension — everywhere, and always.
Flanked by from this time forth and for evermore, Psalm 113:2.
Malachi 1:11 turns the summons into a prophecy of the Gentiles.
usage: from the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD's name is to be praised
blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and for evermore
my name shall be great among the Gentiles

word: He That Diggeth a Pit Shall Fall Into It
pronunciation: hee that DIG-eth uh PIT shal FAWL IN-too it
pos: n. phr. (the Preacher's proverb of recoil, Ecclesiastes 10:8)
etymology: Hebrew chōphēr gūmmāts bō yippōl — chāphar, to dig; gūmmāts, a pit, a word occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible.
biblical_def: The Preacher sets the saying in a short run of workman's proverbs: he that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him; whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby. Read as a group they are about the hazards of the work itself, and the first is sharpened by the fact that in Scripture the dug pit is almost always a trap laid for someone else. The Psalter uses the image repeatedly and with the same outcome: he made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made; his mischief shall return upon his own head. This is not karma, which is an impersonal law of cosmic balance working itself out over lifetimes; it is the moral government of a Person, who has so ordered the world that malice characteristically recoils, and who is free to let it recoil at once, later, or not visibly at all. Ecclesiastes itself is the book most insistent that the recoil is not mechanical — there be just men unto whom it happeneth according to the work of the wicked. Haman hanged on his own gallows is the Bible's plainest illustration, and the Preacher's point is a warning to the digger rather than a comfort to the watching.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Dig, to open and break or turn up the earth. Pit, a deep hole in the earth; a snare. Ecclesiastes 10:8, the trap that takes its maker.
webster_full: Dig, to open and break or turn up the earth with a spade or other instrument.
Pit, a deep hole in the earth; an artificial cavity; figuratively, a snare.
Hedge, a fence of thorn bushes or small trees.
Hebrew chāphar, to dig, search out, explore.
Hebrew gūmmāts, a pit; the word occurs only at Ecclesiastes 10:8.
scriptures: Ecc 10:8
He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him.
Ecc 10:9
Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby.
Psa 7:15
He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made.
Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.
corruption_summary: The proverb is read as a guarantee that wrongdoers are punished in this life, which Ecclesiastes itself denies; or it is absorbed into karma, an impersonal law without a Judge.
corruption_paragraphs: Taken as a rule without exception, the saying promises that the malicious always fall into their own pits here and now, and the believer who watches an unpunished oppressor concludes that Scripture has failed him. Ecclesiastes is the last book that can be used that way. The same Preacher records that there be just men unto whom it happeneth according to the work of the wicked, and that one event happeneth to them all. A proverb states what characteristically happens, not what invariably happens, and the Preacher's own answer to the exceptions is the judgment at the end: God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the difference between this doctrine and karma, with which it is now routinely confused. Karma is an impersonal moral physics, self-operating, requiring no judge and admitting no mercy, and balancing accounts across successive lives. Scripture's recoil is the act of a Person who governs His world, who may suspend the consequence for a season to lead a man to repentance, and who has in Christ taken the recoil of our own digging upon Himself. The two look alike only until one asks whether anybody is minding the scales.
roots_summary: Hebrew chāphar, to dig, with gūmmāts, a pit found only here — the trap that characteristically takes its maker, under a Judge and not a law of physics.
roots_lines: Hebrew chāphar, to dig or search out.
Hebrew gūmmāts, a pit; a hapax legomenon in the Hebrew Bible.
One of four workman's proverbs in Ecclesiastes 10:8-9.
The Psalter's parallel: fallen into the ditch which he made, Psalm 7:15.
Proverbs 26:27 joins the rolled stone that returns upon him.
usage: he that diggeth a pit shall fall into it
whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him
his mischief shall return upon his own head

word: Until the Day Break, and the Shadows Flee Away
pronunciation: un-TIL thuh DAY BRAYK and thuh SHAD-ohz FLEE uh-WAY
pos: n. phr. (the bride's refrain in the Song, 2:17 and 4:6)
etymology: Hebrew 'ad sheyyāphūach hayyōm w'nāsū hats'lālīm — pūach, to breathe or blow, so literally until the day breathes, the Hebrew image for the stirring of the dawn breeze.
biblical_def: The refrain stands twice in the Song, first on the bride's lips and then on the Bridegroom's. The Hebrew is more delicate than the English: not until the day breaks but until the day breathes, the stirring of air that comes before sunrise, while the long shadows of night are still in flight. In 2:17 the bride bids her beloved turn and be like a roe upon the mountains of Bether until that hour; in 4:6 he says he will get him to the mountain of myrrh until the same. The Song is first of all what it presents itself as, the love of a bridegroom and his bride within marriage, and the dictionary takes it so: Solomon's celebration of the one union God made, in a book the canon did not blush to include. Upon that foundation the church has long read the Song also of Christ and His people, as the prophets read Israel the bride and as Paul reads marriage a great mystery concerning Christ and the church. On that reading the refrain names the present age exactly: the shadows have not yet fled, the day has not yet breathed, and the bride speaks to a Beloved she does not yet see. Peter's language is the same — until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Break, of day, to begin to appear; to dawn. Shadow, obscurity; darkness; a faint representation. Song of Solomon 2:17, the refrain of the night that is passing.
webster_full: Break, of the day, to begin to appear; to dawn; to open.
Shadow, shade within defined limits; obscurity; darkness.
Shadow, a faint representation or imperfect image of something to come.
Hebrew pūach, to breathe or blow — until the day breathes.
Hebrew tsēl, a shadow; the plural of the night's fleeing shades.
scriptures: Son 2:17
Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether.
Son 4:6
Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense.
Son 2:16
My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: The Song is stripped of its plain sense and made allegory only, or stripped of its covenant setting and made a celebration of desire detached from marriage.
corruption_paragraphs: The older error, running from Origen through much medieval exposition, was embarrassment at the plain sense: the Song was read as allegory only, and its frank delight in the body of a spouse explained away. That handling cost the church a great deal, since Scripture gives here the one book wholly devoted to married love and the church learned to be ashamed of it. The plain sense is the foundation and the figure is built upon it; an allegory that must deny the letter is not exposition.

The modern error runs the other way and is the more dangerous. The Song is quoted as warrant for desire as such, detached from the covenant that frames it — the bride is a spouse, the book speaks of a wedding, and its own repeated charge is not to stir up love until it please. That refrain is a guard, and a book that contains it cannot be made a charter for passion without vows. The principle to recover is that Scripture holds the two together: a married love celebrated without apology, and a Beloved for whom the bride waits through a night whose shadows have not yet fled.
roots_summary: Hebrew pūach, to breathe — until the day breathes and the night's shadows flee, the refrain of a love that waits.
roots_lines: Hebrew pūach, to breathe or blow; the dawn breeze, not the sunrise itself.
Hebrew ts'lālīm, shadows; nūs, to flee.
The refrain stands twice: Song 2:17 on the bride's lips, 4:6 on the Bridegroom's.
Bether in 2:17 is rendered by some as separation, fitting the refrain.
Compare Peter: until the day dawn, and the day star arise, 2 Peter 1:19.
usage: until the day break, and the shadows flee away
my beloved is mine, and I am his
turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe

word: The Watchmen That Went About the City Found Me
pronunciation: thuh WOCH-mun that WENT uh-BOWT thuh SIT-ee FOWND mee
pos: n. phr. (the bride's second search in the Song, 5:7)
etymology: Hebrew m'tsā'ūnī hashshōm'rīm hassōb'bīm bā'īr — shāmar, to keep or guard, hence the watchmen; sābab, to go round, of their circuit of the walls.
biblical_def: The clause occurs twice and the second time is harder than the first. In Song 3:3 the bride, seeking him whom her soul loveth, meets the watchmen going about the city and asks them simply, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth? In 5:7, after she has been slow to open to her beloved and he has withdrawn, she goes out again and the same men treat her very differently: The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me. The men appointed to guard the city mistake the one person in it who has most right to be out, and the search that cost her nothing the first time costs her blood the second. Taken at the plain level the Song is Solomon's celebration of married love, and this is the night a wife's delay turns into a frightening search. Taken in the figure the church has long seen in the book, the passage is a severe and useful one: the soul that has been slow to open to Christ may find, when it rouses itself at last to seek Him, that He is not immediately found and that even the appointed keepers of the walls wound rather than help. She is not abandoned — the chapter ends with the great description of her Beloved — but she is not spared either.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Watchman, one set to guard a city and prevent danger. Veil, a cover; a curtain; a part of female dress. Song of Solomon 5:7, the keepers who wounded the seeker.
webster_full: Watchman, a sentinel; one set to guard a city or camp and give notice of danger.
Keeper, one who holds or has possession; one who guards or preserves.
Veil, a cover; a curtain; a part of female dress which covers the face.
Hebrew shāmar, to keep, guard, watch over.
Hebrew sābab, to turn about, go round, make a circuit. Song 5:7.
scriptures: Son 3:3
The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?
Son 5:6
I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.
Son 5:7
The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me.
Son 5:8
I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.
corruption_summary: The passage is softened into a bad dream with no meaning, or it is read as proof that the church's officers are simply enemies of the devout soul.
corruption_paragraphs: Many expositors dispose of the scene by calling it a dream and leaving it there. The Song does say I sleep, but my heart waketh, and the dream framing is real; it is not an exemption from meaning. Scripture's dreams carry freight, and this one is placed with care immediately after a refusal: he knocked, she had put off her coat and would not rise, and by the time she opened he had withdrawn himself. The scene that follows is the cost of the delay, and softening it empties the warning the Song means to give.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is a restraint in applying the figure. It is tempting, and now common, to read the watchmen simply as the institutional church and the beating as proof that the fervent soul should expect only harm from pastors and elders. The same book gives watchmen their honourable sense, Isaiah sets watchmen upon the walls who shall never hold their peace, and the New Testament commands obedience to those who watch for souls. What the passage teaches is that keepers can fail, and fail most when they are needed; not that keeping is the enemy. The bride does not renounce the city. She charges its daughters to tell her Beloved that she is sick of love.
roots_summary: Hebrew shāmar, to guard, with sābab, to make a circuit — the city's own keepers wounding the bride on her second and costlier search.
roots_lines: Hebrew shāmar, to keep or guard; the participle gives watchmen.
Hebrew sābab, to go round about — their circuit of the walls.
Hebrew r'dīd, a wide wrapper or veil, taken from her.
The first meeting cost her nothing, Song 3:3; the second drew blood.
The scene follows her refusal to open, Song 5:3 and 5:6.

word: I Will Not Destroy It for Ten's Sake
pronunciation: y wil not dee-STROY it for TENZ SAYK
pos: n. phr. (the end of Abraham's intercession for Sodom, Genesis 18:32)
etymology: Hebrew lō' 'ashchīth ba''būr hā''āsārāh — shāchath, to destroy or corrupt; ba''būr, for the sake of, on account of — the preposition of substitutionary benefit.
biblical_def: Abraham stands yet before the LORD and begins the boldest conversation in Genesis. Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? He asks whether the city will be spared for fifty righteous, and is told it will; then forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and at last ten, each time with the same answer and with the same apology for asking — Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak yet but this once. The final word is the LORD's: And he said, I will not destroy it for ten's sake. Three things are established. The first is the principle of the saving remnant: a handful of righteous within a city are of such weight that their presence would hold back judgment from the whole, which is why Christ calls His people the salt of the earth. The second is the character of God in intercession — it is Abraham who stops at ten, not the LORD who stops him, and every request is granted. The third is the hinge of the narrative: there were not ten, and Sodom fell, yet Lot was taken out first, because God knoweth how to deliver the godly. The passage is therefore not a failed negotiation but a demonstration that the Judge of all the earth does right, which is exactly what Abraham had asked.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Destroy, to demolish; to lay waste; to ruin. Sake, final cause; end; purpose; account. Genesis 18:32, the city spared for ten righteous men.
webster_full: Destroy, to demolish; to pull down; to ruin; to annihilate a city by demolishing.
Sake, final cause; end; purpose; account; as, for the sake of ten.
Intercession, prayer or solicitation to one party in favour of another.
Hebrew shāchath, to destroy, corrupt, lay waste.
Hebrew ba''būr, for the sake of, on account of. Genesis 18:32.
scriptures: That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked: and that the righteous should be as the wicked, that be far from thee: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?
And he said, Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak yet but this once: Peradventure ten shall be found there. And he said, I will not destroy it for ten's sake.
And it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt.
The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished:
corruption_summary: The exchange is read as Abraham bargaining God down from severity, or the passage is taken to prove that God will not finally judge a wicked society.
corruption_paragraphs: The familiar telling makes it a haggle: Abraham, more merciful than God, talks Him down from fifty to ten. The text reverses the roles at every step. The LORD opens the conversation Himself by asking whether He shall hide from Abraham the thing He does, every single request is granted without resistance, and it is Abraham who stops asking. What is being displayed is not divine reluctance overcome but divine mercy drawn out, and the man learning it is the one who will later be asked for his son. A God who must be argued into kindness is not the God of this chapter.

The second misuse takes the passage as a guarantee: there are always some righteous somewhere, therefore judgment never falls. Genesis 19 is the answer, printed immediately after. There were not ten, fire fell, and the cities became an example unto those that after should live ungodly. Yet the same chapter records that God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow — which is Peter's doctrine exactly: the Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished. The principle to recover is that intercession is real, the remnant is weighty, and neither suspends the judgment of a God who does right.
roots_summary: Hebrew shāchath, to destroy, with ba''būr, for the sake of — a whole city held back from judgment on account of ten righteous men.
roots_lines: Hebrew shāchath, to destroy, corrupt, or lay waste.
Hebrew ba''būr, for the sake of — benefit reckoned to one on account of another.
Hebrew tsaddīq, righteous; the ten whose presence would have sufficed.
Abraham stops the asking at ten; the LORD grants every petition.
The outcome and its mercy: God remembered Abraham, Genesis 19:29.

word: I Stand at the Door, and Knock
pronunciation: y STAND at thuh DOR and NOK
pos: n. phr. (Christ's word to the church at Laodicea, Revelation 3:20)
etymology: Greek hestēka epi tēn thyran kai krouō — histēmi in the perfect, I have taken my stand and am standing; krouō, to knock, used of knocking at a door for admission.
biblical_def: The verse closes the last of the seven letters, and its address governs its meaning: it is spoken to a church, not to the unconverted world. Laodicea is lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, and says she is rich and increased with goods and has need of nothing, while Christ calls her wretched, miserable, poor, blind and naked. He counsels her to buy of Him gold tried in the fire, white raiment, and eyesalve; He says that as many as He loves He rebukes and chastens, and bids her be zealous and repent. Then: Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me. The picture is of a congregation that has conducted its affairs so successfully without Him that its Lord is outside His own assembly, asking to be let in. The promise is not of mere entry but of supper — the shared evening meal, the most unhurried and familiar fellowship the ancient world had. And the appeal is individual within the corporate: if any man hear. Where a whole church has shut Him out, the invitation is still open to one person in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Knock, to strike against something with a sharp noise, as at a door for admittance. Sup, to eat the evening meal. Revelation 3:20, Christ outside the church of Laodicea.
webster_full: Knock, to strike or beat with something thick or heavy; to rap, as at a door for admittance.
Sup, to eat the evening meal; to take supper.
Lukewarm, moderately warm; figuratively, indifferent; not ardent.
Greek krouō, to knock, as at a door; histēmi, to stand or take one's stand.
Greek deipneō, to dine or take the chief meal of the day. Revelation 3:20.
scriptures: Rev 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
Rev 3:19
As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.
Rev 3:20
Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.
Rev 3:21
To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne.
corruption_summary: The verse is lifted out of its address to a church and made the standard appeal to the unconverted, with Christ waiting powerless on the sinner's decision; or the knocking is sentimentalised into mere wistfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: Generations of evangelistic preaching, helped by a famous painting, have made this the text for inviting an unbeliever to open his heart's door, with the whole issue hanging on the handle being on the inside. The letter is addressed to the angel of the church of the Laodiceans, and the condition described is not unbelief but complacency in a congregation that thinks itself rich. There are better texts for calling sinners to Christ, and this one has a sharper use: it asks a prosperous and self-satisfied church whether its Lord is inside the building. Where the verse is spent on the unconverted, the professing church never hears the knock aimed at it.

The second corruption follows from the first and is doctrinally graver. The picture is made one of divine helplessness, Christ reduced to a patient suppliant whose success depends entirely on an autonomous human will. The same letter forbids it. Two verses earlier He says, as many as I love, I rebuke and chasten — He is already acting on Laodicea, not merely waiting on her — and He commands her to be zealous and repent, which is the language of a Lord, not a petitioner. The knocking is real and the invitation is sincere; the One knocking is also the One who opens hearts, as He opened Lydia's. The principle to recover is that the courtesy of the knock does not imply the impotence of the Knocker.
roots_summary: Greek histēmi in the perfect, I have taken my stand, with krouō, to knock — Christ outside a self-satisfied church, promising supper to any who open.
roots_lines: Greek histēmi, perfect tense: I have taken my stand and remain standing.
Greek krouō, to knock at a door seeking admittance.
Greek deipneō, to sup — the unhurried evening meal, the figure of fellowship.
The address is to a church: the angel of the church of the Laodiceans, Revelation 3:14.
The individual appeal stands within the corporate: if any man hear my voice.

word: The Stones Would Immediately Cry Out
pronunciation: thuh STOHNZ wuud i-MEE-dee-it-lee KRY OWT
pos: n. phr. (Christ's answer to the Pharisees at the triumphal entry, Luke 19:40)
etymology: Greek hoi lithoi kekraxontai — lithos, a stone; krazō, to cry out with a loud and urgent voice, the verb used of a raven's harsh call and of the shout of a crowd.
biblical_def: As Jesus comes down the descent of the mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples begins to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen, crying, Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord. Certain of the Pharisees say, Master, rebuke thy disciples. And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out. The saying is not a pleasantry. It asserts that the praise of the Messiah entering His city is not optional in the universe — it will be rendered, and if the appointed voices are silenced the creation will supply them. Scripture has prepared the thought: the heavens declare the glory of God, the hills break forth into singing, the stone shall cry out of the wall. Habakkuk's use is the sharpest parallel, where the stone cries out against the builder's injustice, so that the figure carries witness as well as praise. Luke immediately records what follows: Christ beholds the city and weeps over it, saying that the things which belong unto her peace are hid from her eyes. The stones that would have cried out are, within a few verses, the stones of a city of which not one shall be left upon another.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Cry out, to exclaim; to vociferate. Immediately, instantly; without delay. Luke 19:40, the praise that will be rendered though the voices be silenced.
webster_full: Cry out, to exclaim; to utter a loud voice; to vociferate.
Immediately, instantly; at the present time; without intervention of time.
Stone, a hard substance of earthy or mineral matter.
Greek krazō, to cry out with a loud, harsh or urgent voice.
Hold one's peace, to be silent. Luke 19:40.
scriptures: And when he was come nigh, even now at the descent of the mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen;
And some of the Pharisees from among the multitude said unto him, Master, rebuke thy disciples.
And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
Hab 2:11
For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.
corruption_summary: The saying is made a piece of nature-mysticism in which creation worships of itself, or it is used to excuse the silence of the church on the ground that God will manage without her.
corruption_paragraphs: Detached from the scene, the line is quoted as though stones and trees were already worshipping in their own right and human praise were merely one voice in a general chorus. Christ's sentence is conditional and pointed: if these should hold their peace. It is addressed to Pharisees demanding that disciples be silenced, and it says that the Messiah's entry into Jerusalem will be acknowledged one way or another. The creation declares God's glory because He made it to, not because it is itself divine, and Scripture never invites a man to listen to the stones instead of to the word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the verse is a rebuke to the silencers and not a comfort to the silent. It is sometimes used to shrug — if we do not speak, God will raise up someone or something else — which turns a warning into an excuse. The warning runs the other way. Luke sets the saying beside Christ weeping over a city that did not know the time of her visitation, and the next thing He does is cleanse the temple. A generation that leaves the praise to the stones is not relieved of a duty; it is being told what its silence is worth.
roots_summary: Greek krazō, to cry out urgently, of stones — a conditional rebuke to those silencing the disciples, not a doctrine of worshipping creation.
roots_lines: Greek lithos, a stone; krazō, to cry out loudly and urgently.
The sentence is conditional: if these should hold their peace.
Spoken to Pharisees demanding the disciples be rebuked, Luke 19:39.
Habakkuk 2:11 — the stone shall cry out of the wall, as a witness.
Luke places it beside Christ weeping over the city, Luke 19:41.
